title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Electio proper — glory; Thomas; vs praedestinatio
pass_a_gloss: Election therefore, concerning which it will be for us to treat, denotes the singular action of the Divine will from eternity separating certain ones unto the end of glory or of eternal life, others having been passed by. And this election, just as also love, is presupposed to predestination, as Thomas rightly annotated. For all the predestined are understood as elect and beloved: Beloved, insofar as God wills to them the good of eternal life; elect, insofar as he wills to them this good which he does not will to others. Properly therefore and rightly taken, election regards the end alone, and is the Divine will of conferring glory upon certain singular persons, with the passing-by of others. Although it must be confessed that by theologians election is sometimes confused with predestination: But when they are distinguished, election is chiefly and properly referred to the end itself, as has been said; predestination to the means, as will now be shown.
pass_b_english: The election we must treat, then, is the singular act of the Divine will that from eternity sets certain ones apart for the end of glory — eternal life — and passes others by. Thomas rightly notes that this election, like love, is presupposed to predestination. All the predestined are understood as elect and beloved: beloved insofar as God wills them the good of eternal life; elect insofar as he wills them that good and does not will it to others. Taken properly, election looks only to the end: it is God's will to confer glory on particular persons while passing others by. Theologians do sometimes blur election with predestination. When the words are kept apart, election belongs chiefly to the end itself; predestination belongs to the means — as we will now show.
source_text: Electio igitur, de qua nobis agendum erit, denotat singularem actionem voluntatis Divinae ab aeterno separantis quosdam ad finem gloriae seu vitae aeternae, aliis praeteritis. Atque haec electio, sicuti etiam & dilectio, praesupponitur praedestinationi, ut recte annotavit Thomas. Nam omnes praedestinati intelliguntur electi & dilecti: Dilecti, quatenus Deus vult illis bonum aeternae vitae; electi, quatenus vult illis hoc bonum quod non vult aliis. Proprie igitur & recte sumpta electio solum finem respicit, & est voluntas Divina conferendi gloriam singularibus quibusdam personis, cum praeteritione aliorum. Quanquam fatendum est, a Theologis nonnunquam confundi electionem cum praedestinatione: Quando vero distinguuntur, electio praecipue & proprie refertur ad ipsum finem, uti dictum est; praedestinatio ad media, uti nunc ostendetur.
